interview.question: What does KBinsDiscretizer do, and what can encode control?
interview.answer: It converts continuous features into intervals. The learned interval membership is returned as sparse one-hot output by default, dense one-hot output when requested, or integer bin identifiers with ordinal encoding.
interview.followUp: How do the strategies differ? Uniform uses equal widths, quantile targets similarly populated bins, and k-means assigns boundaries from one-dimensional cluster centers.

interview.question: How is n_bins specified and constrained?
interview.answer: n_bins can be one integer applied across features or an array specifying each feature's count. Values below two are invalid.
interview.followUp: What happens when a feature has too few distinct values? The implementation can reduce its effective number of bins; such ignored features are placed to the right of the transformed output.

interview.question: Compare the available binning strategies.
interview.answer: Uniform creates equal-width intervals, quantile creates intervals with approximately equal sample counts, and kmeans uses nearest one-dimensional cluster centers. Each strategy defines boundaries independently for features.
interview.followUp: Why might quantile be sensitive to repeated values? Repeated values can make requested boundaries coincide, reducing the number of effective intervals.

keyPoints: The transformer changes continuous feature values into interval-based representations.
The encode option chooses sparse one-hot, dense one-hot, or ordinal integer output.
The uniform strategy partitions each feature into equal-width bins.
The quantile strategy aims for similarly populated bins in every feature.
The kmeans strategy assigns values according to nearest one-dimensional cluster centers.
Use n_bins as one shared count or provide a per-feature array of counts.
gotchas: Every feature must use at least two bins; smaller values raise ValueError.
Features whose effective bin count is one are not encoded normally and appear at the right side of the transformed output.
Very narrow bins can increase overfitting, so select binning settings inside cross-validation.

KernelPCA.summary: KernelPCA performs nonlinear dimensionality reduction using kernels. It can also learn an approximate inverse mapping back to the original feature space.
KernelPCA.explanation: KernelPCA builds a kernel representation of the samples and extracts principal directions from that representation, enabling nonlinear dimensionality reduction. When inverse transformation is enabled, it learns a regularized mapping from the reduced representation back to the original feature space, so reconstruction is approximate.
KernelPCA.syntax: class sklearn.decomposition.KernelPCA(n_components=None, *, kernel='linear', gamma=None, degree=3, coef0=1, kernel_params=None, alpha=1.0, fit_inverse_transform=False, eigen_solver='auto', tol=0, max_iter=None, iterated_power='auto', remove_zero_eig=False, random_state=None, copy_X=True, n_jobs=None)

parameters.name: n_components
parameters.description: Number of components; None keeps all nonzero components.

parameters.name: kernel
parameters.description: Kernel used for PCA; may be a supported kernel name or callable.

parameters.name: gamma
parameters.description: Kernel coefficient for RBF, polynomial, and sigmoid kernels; None uses 1/n_features.

parameters.name: degree
parameters.description: Degree for polynomial kernels.

parameters.name: coef0
parameters.description: Independent term in polynomial and sigmoid kernels.

parameters.name: kernel_params
parameters.description: Additional parameters for the kernel function.

parameters.name: alpha
parameters.description: Ridge regularization used when learning the inverse transform.

parameters.name: fit_inverse_transform
parameters.description: Whether to learn an inverse transformation.

parameters.name: eigen_solver
parameters.description: Eigensolver selection.

parameters.name: tol
parameters.description: Convergence tolerance for the eigensolver.

parameters.name: max_iter
parameters.description: Maximum eigensolver iterations; None uses the solver default.

parameters.name: iterated_power
parameters.description: Number of power iterations for the randomized solver.

KernelPCA.returns: A fitted KernelPCA transformer; transform returns samples represented in the retained kernel principal components, and inverse_transform returns approximate samples when inverse fitting is enabled.

example.title: Kernel PCA with an RBF kernel
example.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.decomposition import KernelPCA

X, _ = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
transformer = KernelPCA(
    n_components=7,
    kernel="rbf",
    gamma=10,
    fit_inverse_transform=True,
    alpha=0.1,
)
X_transformed = transformer.fit_transform(X)
X_reconstructed = transformer.inverse_transform(X_transformed)
example.explanation: Fits an RBF-kernel projection to the digits data, reduces it to seven components, and computes an approximate reconstruction.

interview.question: What problem does KernelPCA solve, and how does it differ from PCA?
interview.answer: KernelPCA is PCA performed in a kernel-induced representation, so it can discover nonlinear structure that ordinary PCA cannot. The class supports kernels such as linear, polynomial, RBF, sigmoid, cosine, precomputed, or a callable.
interview.followUp: Why can inverse_transform be imperfect? It learns a mapping back to the original feature space rather than applying an analytical inverse, so the result is only an approximation.

interview.question: How does n_components affect the fitted representation?
interview.answer: n_components limits the number of retained components. If it is None, all nonzero components are kept.
interview.followUp: What happens if the requested component count is larger than the available nonzero components? The estimator cannot provide more nonzero components than the kernel decomposition contains.

interview.question: How does KernelPCA compute its components and what controls that computation?
interview.answer: The estimator can use dense, ARPACK, or randomized truncated eigendecomposition depending on eigen_solver and the data. With auto, scikit-learn selects an approach based on input shape and the number of requested components.
interview.followUp: When is inverse_transform useful? Enable fit_inverse_transform to learn a regularized back-mapping, then use inverse_transform for approximate reconstruction.

keyPoints: It extends dimensionality reduction beyond linear projections by applying kernel methods.
The default component setting retains every nonzero component.
The kernel parameter selects the similarity function used to construct the PCA representation.
gamma controls the kernel coefficient for RBF, polynomial, and sigmoid kernels.
degree sets the polynomial degree when the polynomial kernel is selected.
gotchas: Leaving gamma unset makes it depend on the number of input features.

KFold.summary: KFold creates k train/validation splits by holding out each fold once and training on the remaining folds. It can optionally shuffle fold assignment and make that ordering reproducible.
KFold.explanation: KFold divides sample indices into a chosen number of consecutive folds and repeatedly returns one fold as validation data while using the remaining folds for training. Shuffling is optional; when enabled, an integer random_state makes the resulting fold ordering reproducible.

parameters.name: n_splits
parameters.description: Number of folds; must be at least 2.

parameters.name: shuffle
parameters.description: Whether to shuffle data before assigning samples to folds.

parameters.name: random_state

parameters.description: Controls fold-index randomness when shuffle is enabled; otherwise it has no effect.

KFold.returns: A cross-validator whose split method yields training and validation indices.

example.title: Generate K-fold splits
example.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold

X = [[1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6]]
kf = KFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

for train_index, test_index in kf.split(X):
    print(train_index, test_index)
example.explanation: Creates three shuffled, reproducible folds and prints the training and validation indices for each split.

interview.question: What does KFold do?
interview.answer: KFold is a cross-validator that yields train/test index arrays. It partitions the data into n_splits folds and uses each fold once for validation while training on the others.
interview.followUp: How would you make the splits reproducible? Enable shuffle and pass an integer random_state.

interview.question: What is the role of n_splits?
interview.answer: n_splits controls how many folds are created and must be at least 2. Each validation iteration uses one fold, so the number of generated train/test splits equals n_splits.
interview.followUp: What happens when the sample count is not divisible by n_splits? The first n_samples % n_splits folds contain one more sample than the others.

interview.question: How do shuffle and random_state interact?
interview.answer: By default, KFold creates consecutive folds without shuffling. With shuffle=True, it changes the ordering of indices used to form folds; random_state can control that randomness.
interview.followUp: Does shuffle=True randomize the order within each returned train or test split? No—the documentation states that samples within each split are not shuffled.

keyPoints: KFold is a cross-validator for repeatedly producing training and validation index sets.
Its split operation returns indices rather than transformed feature or target data.
The default partitioning forms consecutive folds and leaves the input order unchanged.
Every fold serves once as validation, with all other folds used for training in that iteration.
n_splits cannot be less than two.
An integer random_state provides reproducible shuffled splits across repeated calls.
gotchas: Setting shuffle=True randomizes the fold ordering before splitting, but does not shuffle samples inside an individual split.
random_state only affects results when shuffle=True; leaving shuffling disabled makes it irrelevant.

KMeans.summary: KMeans partitions data into a chosen number of clusters by iteratively assigning samples to centroids and updating those centroids. It supports k-means++ or custom initialization and Lloyd or Elkan optimization.
KMeans.explanation: KMeans partitions samples into a requested number of groups by iteratively assigning points to centroids and updating those centroids. It supports Lloyd’s classical method and Elkan’s triangle-inequality variant, and exposes labels, centers, inertia, and iteration information after fitting.

example.title: Cluster points with KMeans
example.code:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

X = [[1, 2], [1, 4], [1, 0], [10, 2], [10, 4], [10, 0]]

interview.question: How does KMeans form clusters?
interview.answer: KMeans creates the requested number of centroids, assigns each sample to a centroid, and updates centroids repeatedly. It stops when convergence criteria are met or the iteration limit is reached.
interview.followUp: When can Elkan be preferable? It can be faster when clusters are well defined because it uses the triangle inequality, provided the extra memory is acceptable.

interview.question: What does n_clusters control?
interview.answer: n_clusters controls both the number of groups and the number of centroids generated. The default is 8, so it should be set to a value appropriate for the problem.
interview.followUp: What is a consequence of choosing too many clusters? The model creates more centroids and can increase computation while producing a less useful partition.

interview.question: How do initialization and random_state affect fitting?
interview.answer: The default initialization is k-means++, which selects initial centroids using an empirical probability distribution related to points’ contribution to inertia. The random_state parameter controls centroid-initialization randomness.
interview.followUp: How can reproducibility be improved? Supply a fixed random_state and keep the initialization and other configuration unchanged.

keyPoints: KMeans is an unsupervised estimator for partitioning observations into clusters.
n_clusters sets both the requested cluster count and the number of centroids.
init selects how initial centroid positions are obtained; supported choices include k-means++, random, a callable, or an array.
max_iter caps the iterations performed during one run.
tol determines convergence from the relative change between centers on successive iterations.
random_state controls randomness used while initializing centroids.
algorithm selects between Lloyd’s and Elkan’s implementations.
gotchas: Elkan can improve efficiency for well-separated clusters, but its extra distance-related array increases memory use.
Choose Lloyd when the additional memory required by Elkan is undesirable.
Runtime depends on the cluster count, sample count, and number of iterations, so large datasets or many clusters can be costly.

interview.question: How does KNeighborsClassifier make a prediction?
interview.answer: KNeighborsClassifier predicts by applying a vote among the nearest training samples. With uniform weights, every neighbor contributes equally; with distance weights, closer samples contribute more.
interview.followUp: How would you make nearby observations matter more? Set weights="distance", which uses inverse-distance weighting.

interview.question: What does n_neighbors control?
interview.answer: n_neighbors sets the default number of neighbors used for neighbor queries. Increasing it generally includes a broader local region in the vote, while decreasing it makes the decision more local.
interview.followUp: What should be validated rather than assumed? Tune n_neighbors using validation data because the appropriate value depends on the dataset.

interview.question: How do metric and p affect neighborhood selection?
interview.answer: The default metric is Minkowski, and p=2 gives the standard Euclidean distance. Setting p=1 produces Manhattan distance, while other positive p values produce other Minkowski distances.
interview.followUp: How can computation be selected? algorithm="auto" lets the estimator choose among supported neighbor-search approaches based on the fitted data and parameters.

keyPoints: It is a supervised classifier that assigns labels through a k-nearest-neighbor vote.
n_neighbors defaults to 5 and determines the neighborhood size used by default.
weights controls how each neighbor contributes to the predicted class.
Distance weighting gives closer training points greater influence.
algorithm selects how nearest neighbors are computed and defaults to auto.
The default Minkowski metric becomes Euclidean distance when p equals 2.
leaf_size is passed to tree-based neighbor structures and can affect construction, query speed, and memory.
gotchas: The Minkowski power p must be positive.
Choose leaf_size experimentally because its best value depends on the problem.

interview.question: How does KNeighborsRegressor produce a prediction?
interview.answer: KNeighborsRegressor predicts by local interpolation of target values from the nearest training samples. With uniform weights, every selected neighbor contributes equally; with distance weights, closer samples contribute more.
interview.followUp: How would you make the estimator emphasize nearby observations? Use `weights="distance"`, or supply a callable that maps distances to weights.

interview.question: What does n_neighbors control?
interview.answer: `n_neighbors` sets how many neighbors are used by default for neighbor queries. A smaller value makes predictions more local, while a larger value incorporates more training observations.
interview.followUp: What trade-off does changing this value create? Smaller neighborhoods can be more sensitive to local variation, whereas larger neighborhoods smooth predictions over a broader region.

interview.question: Which neighbor-search algorithms can be selected?
interview.answer: The `algorithm` parameter selects among `auto`, `ball_tree`, `kd_tree`, and `brute`. `auto` attempts to choose the most appropriate method from the values passed to `fit`.
interview.followUp: Which distance family is used by default? The default metric is Minkowski with `p=2`, corresponding to Euclidean distance.

Each prediction is formed by interpolating target values belonging to the nearest training points.
`n_neighbors` specifies the default count of neighbors considered for neighbor queries.
`weights` determines how each selected neighbor influences the prediction.
Distance weighting gives nearer observations greater influence through inverse-distance weights.
The `algorithm` option controls the method used to locate nearest neighbors.
`p` is the Minkowski-distance power parameter.
Values of `p` other than the common special cases produce the corresponding Minkowski distance.
gotchas: The `p` value changes the Minkowski distance: 1 gives Manhattan distance, while 2 gives Euclidean distance.
`algorithm="auto"` delegates the neighbor-search method choice to the estimator.

LabelEncoder.summary: LabelEncoder converts target labels into integer codes from 0 to n_classes - 1 and can convert those codes back. It is for y, not input features X.
LabelEncoder.explanation: LabelEncoder learns the distinct values in a target array and stores them in classes_. It maps each value to an integer from 0 through the number of classes minus 1, and inverse_transform converts those integers back to the original labels.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Target values used to fit the encoder; an array-like collection with one value per sample.

LabelEncoder.returns: fit returns the fitted LabelEncoder; transform and fit_transform return an ndarray of encoded labels; inverse_transform returns the original labels.

example.title: Encode and decode target labels
example.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder

encoder = LabelEncoder()
encoded = encoder.fit_transform(["paris", "tokyo", "paris"])
print(encoded.tolist())
print(encoder.classes_.tolist())
print(encoder.inverse_transform(encoded).tolist())
example.explanation: Fits the encoder, converts target labels to integer codes, and restores the original labels.

interview.question: What problem does LabelEncoder solve?
interview.answer: LabelEncoder is intended for encoding the prediction target y. It learns the unique target values and represents them with integers from 0 to n_classes - 1.
interview.followUp: How would you encode categorical input features? Use a feature-oriented encoder such as OneHotEncoder or OrdinalEncoder instead of LabelEncoder.

interview.question: Explain the main LabelEncoder operations.
interview.answer: fit learns the labels and stores them in classes_. transform maps labels to their learned integer codes, while fit_transform performs fitting and encoding in one operation.
interview.followUp: What does inverse_transform do? It maps encoded integers back to the corresponding original labels using the learned class mapping.

interview.question: What does classes_ represent?
interview.answer: The classes_ attribute contains the label for each class, and the encoded values correspond to the positions of those classes. The documentation's examples show both numeric and non-numeric labels being converted and then recovered.
interview.followUp: What must hold for string labels? They must be hashable and comparable so the encoder can process them.

keyPoints: The class converts target labels into consecutive integer codes beginning at zero.
After fitting, classes_ records the distinct target labels known to the encoder.
fit_transform learns the label mapping and returns the encoded target values in one step.
Labels such as strings can be encoded as well as numeric values.
inverse_transform can recover original labels from their encoded integer representations.
gotchas: Use LabelEncoder for target values rather than feature columns; feature encoding requires a different preprocessing approach.
Non-numeric labels are supported only when their values can be both hashed and compared.

Lasso.summary: Lasso is a linear regression estimator with an L1 penalty. It encourages sparse coefficients by allowing some feature weights to become exactly zero.
Lasso.explanation: Lasso fits a linear regression model while adding an L1 penalty to the coefficient vector. The penalty encourages sparse solutions, so some coefficients can become exactly zero; scikit-learn fits the model with coordinate descent.

from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso

X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [2, 2]]

interview.question: What objective does Lasso optimize?
interview.answer: Lasso minimizes squared-error loss plus an L1 penalty, written as [1m(1 / (2 * n_samples)) * ||y - Xw||^2_2 + alpha * ||w||_1[0m. The alpha parameter controls the penalty strength and therefore the sparsity of the learned coefficients.
interview.followUp: What happens when alpha is zero? It becomes ordinary least squares; the documentation recommends LinearRegression for that case.

interview.question: Why use Lasso instead of unregularized linear regression?
interview.answer: Lasso is a linear model that can set coefficients exactly to zero, producing a sparse model. This can reduce the number of features on which predictions depend.
interview.followUp: Which parameter controls this behavior? alpha controls the degree of sparsity: larger regularization generally favors fewer nonzero coefficients.

interview.question: Which optimization algorithm does Lasso use?
interview.answer: The estimator uses coordinate descent to fit the coefficients. Its constructor supports cyclic or random feature selection through selection, with cyclic as the default.
interview.followUp: When can random selection help? With a sufficiently small tolerance, random coordinate selection can sometimes converge faster than cyclic selection.

keyPoints: Lasso is a linear regression estimator with an L1 regularization term.
Its objective combines normalized squared error with alpha times the L1 norm of the coefficients.
The fitted model can produce sparse coefficients, including coefficients exactly equal to zero.
Increasing the regularization strength through alpha changes how sparse the coefficient vector tends to be.
Coefficient fitting is performed using coordinate descent.
Lasso corresponds to ElasticNet with l1_ratio set to 1.0, meaning it has no L2 penalty.
gotchas: An alpha value of zero removes the L1 regularization; use LinearRegression instead for ordinary least squares.
For performance-sensitive fitting, pass X as a Fortran-contiguous NumPy array to avoid unnecessary memory duplication.

LassoCV.explanation: LassoCV fits Lasso models across a regularization path and uses cross-validation to select the best penalty value. It uses coordinate descent, warm-starting each candidate from the closest previously fitted model to make path computation more efficient.

example.title: Select a Lasso penalty by cross-validation
example.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV

X, y = make_regression(n_samples=80, n_features=10, noise=4, random_state=0)

interview.question: What does LassoCV select?
interview.answer: LassoCV evaluates Lasso models over a regularization path and chooses the alpha with the best cross-validation result. Its objective combines squared prediction error with an L1 penalty on coefficients.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from LassoLarsCV? LassoCV uses coordinate descent, whereas LassoLarsCV uses the LARS algorithm.

interview.question: How does `cv` affect fitting?
interview.answer: The `cv` parameter controls the cross-validation splitting strategy. With `None`, the default five-fold strategy is used; an integer specifies the number of folds, while a splitter or iterable can provide explicit splits.
interview.followUp: Why might explicit splits matter? They let the evaluation respect a domain-specific grouping or ordering scheme instead of ordinary folds.

interview.question: What do `eps` and `alphas` control?
interview.answer: `eps` controls the length of the automatically generated alpha path as the ratio of the smallest to largest alpha. The default is `1e-3`, and `alphas` controls how many alpha values are considered, defaulting to 100 in the documented signature.
interview.followUp: What is the trade-off in increasing the number of alphas? It explores the path more finely but increases computation.

keyPoints: It fits a sequence of Lasso models along a regularization path.
Cross-validation determines which candidate penalty produces the selected model.
Its optimization balances squared residual error against an L1 coefficient penalty.
`eps` controls the span of the generated penalty path.
`cv` chooses how training and validation partitions are made.
The estimator fits its Lasso models using coordinate descent.
gotchas: The selected model depends on cross-validation performance rather than a manually fixed penalty.
Path fitting reuses coefficients from a nearby penalty, so the estimator is designed to fit the sequence jointly rather than as unrelated models.

LatentDirichletAllocation.explanation: The estimator learns topic-word weights from a non-negative document-term matrix with variational Bayesian inference. After fitting, transform maps documents to topic mixtures, while components_ stores the learned topic-term weights; batch and online updates support full-data and mini-batch training.

from sklearn.datasets import make_multilabel_classification
from sklearn.decomposition import LatentDirichletAllocation

X, _ = make_multilabel_classification(random_state=0)
lda = LatentDirichletAllocation(n_components=5, random_state=0)

interview.question: What does LatentDirichletAllocation learn and produce?
interview.answer: It is a topic-model estimator that uses online variational Bayes and supports both batch and online updates. For a document-term matrix, it learns topic-term weights and can infer document-topic representations.
interview.followUp: How would you train on sequentially available data? Use partial_fit, which the documentation identifies for data fetched sequentially.

interview.question: How do components_ and transform relate?
interview.answer: components_ stores the topic-term matrix learned from the input. transform computes the document-topic matrix for documents.
interview.followUp: What is the corresponding matrix shape? components_ has shape (n_components, n_features), while transformed data has shape (n_samples, n_components).

interview.question: What is the difference between batch and online learning?
interview.answer: learning_method controls updates: batch uses full passes through the data, while online uses mini-batches. learning_decay and learning_offset control the online learning rate.
interview.followUp: When is online training especially useful? It is useful when data can be fetched sequentially and processed incrementally with partial_fit.

keyPoints: The estimator models latent topics with online variational Bayes.
n_components sets how many topics the model learns.
learning_method selects batch or online parameter updates.
For online learning, learning_decay and learning_offset govern the learning-rate schedule.
The learned topic-term representation is stored in components_.
transform produces document-topic representations for input documents.
partial_fit supports incremental training when data is obtained sequentially.
gotchas: The online method is intended for mini-batch updates; use partial_fit when data arrives sequentially.
Online training's result and convergence speed can vary with mini-batch size and learning-rate settings.

learning_curve.summary: Computes cross-validated training and test scores for multiple training-set sizes. It helps assess how estimator performance changes as more training data is provided.
learning_curve.explanation: The function clones and fits the estimator repeatedly on progressively sized subsets of the training data. For every size, it evaluates both training and held-out test partitions across the cross-validation splits, then returns the scores; optional timing arrays are included when requested.
learning_curve.syntax: sklearn.model_selection.learning_curve(estimator, X, y, *, groups=None, train_sizes=array([0.1, 0.33, 0.55, 0.78, 1.]), cv=None, scoring=None, exploit_incremental_learning=False, n_jobs=None, pre_dispatch='all', verbose=0, shuffle=False, random_state=None, error_score=nan, return_times=False, params=None)

example.title: Evaluate learning curves
example.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
model = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0)
sizes, train_scores, test_scores = learning_curve(
    model, X, y, cv=5, train_sizes=[0.2, 0.5, 1.0],
    scoring="accuracy", n_jobs=-1
)
print(sizes)
print(test_scores.mean(axis=1))
example.explanation: Computes cross-validated training and test accuracy for three training-set sizes.

interview.question: What does learning_curve return?
interview.answer: learning_curve evaluates an estimator at several training-set sizes. For each size, it performs cross-validation, computes training and test scores, and averages those scores across folds.
interview.followUp: How can fit and scoring costs be measured? Set return_times=True; the result then includes fit-time and score-time arrays in addition to sizes and scores.

interview.question: What are the main controls for the experiment?
interview.answer: train_sizes specifies the evaluated training-set sizes, either as relative fractions or absolute counts. cv controls the splitting strategy, while scoring selects the metric used for training and test evaluation.
interview.followUp: What happens when scoring is omitted? The estimator's default scoring method is used.

interview.question: What inputs does the function require?
interview.answer: The estimator must provide fit because it is cloned and trained repeatedly. X contains the features, and y contains the corresponding classification or regression targets, or can be None where supported.
interview.followUp: Why is cloning useful? It gives each validation run an independent unfitted estimator, preventing state from leaking between runs.

keyPoints: Use learning_curve to study how model performance changes as progressively larger training sets are used.
Each requested size creates a smaller or larger subset for fitting within every cross-validation run.
Scores are aggregated across folds separately for each training-size value.
The scoring argument determines the metric applied to both the training and held-out test portions.
gotchas: Values in train_sizes may be relative fractions or absolute example counts; the function uses them to select the training-set sizes.
The chosen cross-validation strategy determines how the data is partitioned for each repeated fit and evaluation.
The supplied estimator must implement fit and is cloned separately for each validation run.

LeaveOneOut.summary: LeaveOneOut is a cross-validator that holds out one sample at a time while using all remaining samples for training. It creates as many splits as there are samples.
LeaveOneOut.explanation: LeaveOneOut generates one train/test split for every sample. In each split, exactly one sample is the test set and all other samples are used for training, so the number of splits equals the number of samples.
LeaveOneOut.returns: An iterator yielding pairs of train and test index arrays.

example.title: Iterate leave-one-out splits
example.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import LeaveOneOut

X = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]])
y = np.array([0, 1, 1])
loo = LeaveOneOut()

for train_idx, test_idx in loo.split(X, y):
    print("train:", train_idx, "test:", test_idx)
example.explanation: Creates one split per sample and prints the training and singleton test indices.

useCases.title: Small-sample validation
useCases.scenario: Estimating model performance when the dataset is small and retaining nearly all observations for each training run matters.

useCases.title: Observation sensitivity
useCases.scenario: Inspecting how predictions change when each individual observation is omitted.

useCases.title: Custom cross-validation loops
useCases.scenario: Generating explicit train/test index pairs for custom evaluation loops.

interview.question: How does LeaveOneOut construct its splits?
interview.answer: LeaveOneOut is a cross-validator that creates one split for each sample. The held-out test set contains one sample, while every other sample forms the training set.
interview.followUp: How many splits are produced for n samples? Exactly n splits, because each sample is held out once.

interview.question: What does LeaveOneOut return?
interview.answer: Its test sets are singletons, and the corresponding training sets contain all remaining samples. The splitter returns train and test indices rather than fitting an estimator itself.
interview.followUp: What does split return? It yields pairs of index arrays identifying the training and test rows for each fold.

interview.question: How does LeaveOneOut relate to other cross-validation splitters?
interview.answer: LeaveOneOut is equivalent to KFold with n_splits equal to the number of samples and to LeavePOut with p equal to 1. Its main drawback is the potentially high computation cost.
interview.followUp: When might another strategy be preferable? For large datasets, use a cross-validation method with fewer folds to reduce repeated model fitting.

keyPoints: Use it as an index generator for repeatedly separating training rows from held-out rows.
Every fold tests exactly one observation, with all other observations available for training.
The same partitioning can be expressed with KFold using one fold per sample or LeavePOut with one omitted sample.
gotchas: It can be computationally expensive because it trains and evaluates once for every sample.

interview.question: What objective does LinearRegression optimize?
interview.answer: LinearRegression fits an ordinary least-squares linear model. It chooses coefficients and an intercept that minimize the residual sum of squares between observed and predicted targets.
interview.followUp: How can coefficient signs be constrained? Set positive=True, which requires non-negative coefficients and uses a non-negative least-squares approach.

interview.question: How is the estimator used after construction?
interview.answer: fit(X, y, sample_weight=None) learns the model from feature matrix X and target y. After fitting, predict(X) returns predictions for new samples.
interview.followUp: What happens with multiple targets? The estimator supports multi-output regression by fitting a coefficient set for each target.

interview.question: What input and positivity considerations matter?
interview.answer: The estimator can fit dense or sparse input. With positive=True, coefficients are constrained to be positive, and sparse input is not supported for that mode.
interview.followUp: Which diagnostic can identify redundant feature directions? Inspect rank_ and singular_ when the fitted input is sufficiently compatible with those attributes.

interview.question: What is LinearSVC and when would you choose it over SVC with a linear kernel?
interview.answer: LinearSVC is a linear support-vector classifier implemented with liblinear. Compared with SVC using a linear kernel, it offers different penalty and loss choices and is intended to scale better to many samples.
interview.followUp: How are multiclass problems handled? The estimator trains one classifier per class in a one-vs-the-rest scheme.

interview.question: How does C affect LinearSVC?
interview.answer: C controls the regularization strength inversely: smaller values apply stronger regularization, while larger values allow the model to fit the training data more closely. The default is 1.0.
interview.followUp: What does class_weight do? It changes the weight of classes in the objective; balanced weighting derives weights from class frequencies.

interview.question: Which learned attributes and prediction methods are useful after fitting?
interview.answer: The estimator exposes coef_ for the learned feature weights and intercept_ for the intercept. decision_function returns confidence scores, while predict maps samples to class labels.
interview.followUp: What is a useful sparse-model configuration? Select penalty='l1' with a compatible loss to obtain sparse coefficient vectors.

keyPoints: It provides a linear SVM alternative to SVC(kernel='linear') while using the liblinear implementation.
Training accepts both dense feature matrices and sparse representations.
For multiple classes, it fits one binary model per class against all remaining classes.
L1 regularization can produce sparse feature-weight vectors, which may help with feature selection.
With dual set to auto, the solver selects the primal or dual formulation based on the problem dimensions and related settings.
C is the main regularization trade-off parameter and defaults to 1.0.
gotchas: Not every penalty and loss combination is valid; in particular, L1 regularization cannot be paired with hinge loss.

interview.question: What does load_digits load, and what can it return?
interview.answer: The function loads a classification dataset in which each sample is an 8×8 digit image. Its default return value is a Bunch, while return_X_y=True gives the feature matrix and target separately.
interview.followUp: What shape does the feature matrix use? Each image is flattened into 64 features, while the Bunch also exposes the image-shaped representation.

interview.question: What is the purpose and valid range of n_class?
interview.answer: n_class controls how many classes are returned and defaults to 10. The documented valid range is 0 through 10.
interview.followUp: Why might a caller use fewer classes? To create a smaller, restricted classification task for experiments or demonstrations.

LocallyLinearEmbedding.summary: LocallyLinearEmbedding learns a low-dimensional representation by preserving local neighborhood relationships. Its method parameter supports standard, Hessian, modified, and local tangent-space alignment variants.
LocallyLinearEmbedding.explanation: The estimator finds each sample’s nearest neighbors, computes weights that reconstruct the sample from that local neighborhood, and then chooses a low-dimensional representation that preserves those local reconstruction relationships. The selected method controls the LLE variant, while the estimator exposes the result through fit_transform and reports reconstruction_error_.
LocallyLinearEmbedding.syntax: class sklearn.manifold.LocallyLinearEmbedding(*, n_neighbors=5, n_components=2, reg=0.001, eigen_solver='auto', tol=1e-06, max_iter=100, method='standard', hessian_tol=0.0001, modified_tol=1e-12, neighbors_algorithm='auto', random_state=None, n_jobs=None)

parameters.description: Number of neighbors used to construct each local neighborhood; default 5.

parameters.name: n_components
parameters.description: Number of coordinates in the learned embedding; default 2.

parameters.name: reg

parameters.name: eigen_solver

parameters.name: tol
parameters.description: Tolerance for the eigenvalue solver; default 1e-6.

parameters.name: max_iter

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: Embedding algorithm: standard, hessian, modified, or ltsa; default standard.

parameters.name: hessian_tol

parameters.name: modified_tol
parameters.description: Tolerance used by modified LLE; default 1e-12.

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.manifold import LocallyLinearEmbedding

interview.question: What does LLE optimize conceptually?
interview.answer: LLE preserves local neighborhood structure rather than global pairwise distances. Standard LLE performs nearest-neighbor search, constructs local reconstruction weights, and solves a partial eigenvalue problem for the embedding.
interview.followUp: How does the modified variant differ operationally? The documentation identifies modified LLE as a separate algorithm selected with method='modified'.

interview.question: Which algorithm variants can LocallyLinearEmbedding use?
interview.answer: The method parameter selects standard, hessian, modified, or ltsa. The default is standard, and each option represents a different locally based embedding procedure.
interview.followUp: Which setting enables local tangent space alignment? Set method='ltsa'.

interview.question: How do n_neighbors and n_components affect configuration?
interview.answer: n_neighbors controls the local neighborhood size, while n_components specifies the number of output coordinates. The hessian variant additionally requires a sufficiently large neighborhood relative to the requested dimensionality.
interview.followUp: What should be checked when a Hessian configuration fails? Verify the documented inequality between n_neighbors and n_components.

keyPoints: LocallyLinearEmbedding is the object-oriented estimator for producing a locally linear manifold embedding.
The estimator supports four algorithm choices, with standard used unless another method is selected.
The standard option applies the original LLE procedure.
The modified option selects the modified LLE algorithm.
The ltsa option uses local tangent space alignment.
The class provides an estimator-style alternative to the functional locally_linear_embedding API.
gotchas: The hessian method has a minimum-neighborhood constraint: n_neighbors must exceed n_components multiplied by 1 plus the triangular-term expression.

LocalOutlierFactor.summary: LocalOutlierFactor is an unsupervised estimator for detecting observations whose local density is substantially lower than that of their nearest neighbors. It uses k-nearest-neighbor distances to compute local outlier scores.
LocalOutlierFactor.explanation: LOF estimates each sample’s local density from its nearest neighbors, then compares that density with neighboring densities. Samples that are substantially less dense than their surroundings receive stronger abnormality scores and can be labeled as outliers.
LocalOutlierFactor.syntax: class sklearn.neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor(*, n_neighbors=20, algorithm='auto', leaf_size=30, metric='minkowski', p=2, metric_params=None, contamination='auto', novelty=False, n_jobs=None)

parameters.name: n_neighbors

parameters.description: Leaf size passed to the tree-based neighbor search.

parameters.name: metric
parameters.description: Distance metric used for neighbor searches.

parameters.name: p
parameters.description: Power parameter for the Minkowski metric.

parameters.name: metric_params
parameters.description: Additional keyword arguments for the metric function.

parameters.description: Expected proportion of outliers, or 'auto'.

parameters.name: novelty
parameters.description: Enables novelty detection for unseen data when set before fitting.

parameters.name: n_jobs
parameters.description: Number of parallel jobs used for neighbor search; None means one job.

example.title: Detect training-set outliers
example.code:
from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor

X = [[1.0, 1.0], [1.1, 1.0], [0.9, 1.1], [1.0, 0.9], [8.0, 8.0]]
lof = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=3, contamination="auto")
labels = lof.fit_predict(X)
print(labels)  # -1 denotes an outlier; 1 denotes an inlier

interview.question: What does LocalOutlierFactor measure?
interview.answer: LOF is an unsupervised outlier detector that compares a sample’s local density with the densities around it. A sample is treated as anomalous when its density is substantially lower than that of its neighbors.
interview.followUp: How does LOF define locality? It uses k-nearest neighbors, with distances estimating local density.

interview.question: How is LOF used for ordinary outlier detection?
interview.answer: The default workflow is to call fit_predict on the data being examined. The result labels inliers and outliers, while negative_outlier_factor_ exposes abnormality scores for training samples.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect new data? Construct the estimator with novelty=True before fitting, then use its prediction and scoring methods.

interview.question: What role does n_neighbors play?
interview.answer: n_neighbors controls the neighborhood used for the density comparison. A value of 20 is the documented default, while the appropriate value depends on the local cluster structure.
interview.followUp: What trade-off does changing it create? Smaller neighborhoods emphasize finer local structure; larger neighborhoods produce a broader density comparison.

keyPoints: This class detects unusual observations without requiring labeled training targets.
Each sample receives a LOF-based abnormality score.
The method compares a point’s density with the density of nearby points.
Neighborhood size and distance determine the local density estimate.
Outlier detection is based on a relative, rather than global, density comparison.
Samples substantially less dense than their neighbors are identified as outliers.

log_loss.explanation: The function compares each true class with the probability assigned to it and averages the resulting negative log-likelihoods by default. It accepts binary or multiclass probabilities, optionally applies sample weights, and can return either the mean or the total loss.

parameters.description: Whether to return the mean instead of the sum of per-sample losses.

parameters.name: sample_weight
parameters.description: Per-sample contribution weights.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description: Class labels used to interpret the probability columns; inferred from y_true when omitted.

from sklearn.metrics import log_loss

 y_true = [0, 0, 1, 1]
y_proba = [[0.9, 0.1], [0.8, 0.2], [0.3, 0.7], [0.01, 0.99]]

score = log_loss(y_true, y_proba)

interview.question: What does log_loss measure?
interview.answer: log_loss measures the negative log-likelihood of the true labels under predicted probabilities. Lower values are better because confident probability assigned to the correct class reduces the penalty.
interview.followUp: Why can a confidently wrong prediction be worse than an uncertain one? The logarithm makes assigning near-zero probability to the true class produce a large loss.

interview.question: What is the effect of normalize?
interview.answer: By default, normalize=True returns the mean loss per sample. Setting normalize=False returns the sum of the per-sample losses.
interview.followUp: When would the sum be useful? It preserves the total weighted objective, whereas the mean is easier to compare across datasets with different sample counts.

interview.question: What input format does y_proba use?
interview.answer: y_proba can be a probability matrix with shape (n_samples, n_classes), or a one-dimensional array for binary classification. Its values should represent classifier probabilities, typically obtained from predict_proba.
interview.followUp: How can class interpretation be made explicit? Pass labels to define the class labels used for interpreting the probability columns.

keyPoints: This metric is also called logistic loss or cross-entropy loss.
Use it for binary or multiclass classification, not a one-label target.
Predicted probabilities may be a multiclass matrix or a one-dimensional binary array.
The default output is the average loss across samples.
Set normalize=False to obtain the aggregate loss.
gotchas: At least two distinct labels are required.
Pass probabilities rather than hard class predictions.
Supply labels when inference from the true labels is insufficient, especially with omitted classes.

interview.question: What does LogisticRegression implement?
interview.answer: It is a classifier that fits regularized logistic regression. Regularization is enabled by default, and the available solvers determine which penalty and multiclass formulation can be used.
interview.followUp: Which solver supports elastic-net regularization? The documentation specifies saga only.

interview.question: How does C affect the fitted model?
interview.answer: C is the inverse regularization-strength parameter: smaller values impose stronger regularization, while larger values impose weaker regularization. The parameter is positive and defaults to 1.0.
interview.followUp: What should be checked after changing C? Verify that the chosen solver and penalty combination remains supported.

interview.question: How does solver choice affect multiclass classification?
interview.answer: For at least three classes, every solver except liblinear optimizes penalized multinomial loss. Liblinear is limited to binary classification unless used inside OneVsRestClassifier.
interview.followUp: How can liblinear be used for multiclass data? Wrap the estimator with OneVsRestClassifier to train one binary model per class.

keyPoints: The class trains a logistic-regression classifier with multiple optimization backends.
A penalty is active unless configured otherwise, so the unregularized case must be requested explicitly.
Feature matrices may be supplied as dense arrays or sparse matrices.
With three or more classes, non-liblinear solvers use penalized multinomial loss.
These four solvers restrict the penalty to L2 or no penalty.
Liblinear supports L1 and L2, but its dual formulation is available only with L2.
gotchas: Choose saga when using an elastic-net penalty; other solvers do not support that combination.
Do not use liblinear directly for native multiclass optimization; wrap it with OneVsRestClassifier instead.
Prefer C-contiguous dense arrays or 64-bit CSR matrices to avoid conversion and copying.

interview.question: What kind of data does make_classification generate?
interview.answer: make_classification generates a random n-class classification problem. It builds Gaussian clusters around vertices of an informative-dimensional hypercube, assigns clusters to classes, and can add feature dependence and noise.
interview.followUp: How can you create multiple clusters per class? Set n_clusters_per_class to the desired number, subject to the documented relationship between clusters, classes, and informative dimensions.

interview.question: What does the function return?
interview.answer: With return_X_y=True, the function returns X and y: X has shape (n_samples, n_features), and y contains integer class-membership labels. Setting return_X_y=False returns a Bunch containing the generated data and target.
interview.followUp: What should code do if it needs named fields rather than tuple unpacking? Set return_X_y=False and access the returned Bunch fields.

interview.question: How do the feature categories differ?
interview.answer: n_informative controls the features used to construct the class structure, while n_redundant contains linear combinations of informative features and n_repeated contains duplicates. Remaining features are random noise.
interview.followUp: How can the feature ordering be inspected? Disable shuffling; the documentation specifies the order of informative, redundant, repeated, then noise features.

keyPoints: Use it to synthesize labeled classification data for experiments, demonstrations, and estimator tests.
Class structure starts as normally distributed clusters positioned around hypercube vertices.
The generator can make the problem harder through dependent features and several noise mechanisms.
Features not designated informative, redundant, or repeated carry random noise.
n_samples controls how many rows are generated.
n_features determines the width of the generated feature matrix.
weights controls the class proportions when constructing the target labels.

make_column_transformer.summary: Creates a ColumnTransformer from transformer-and-column pairs without requiring explicit transformer names. Names are generated automatically from transformer types.
make_column_transformer.explanation: The function accepts transformer-and-column pairs, then constructs a ColumnTransformer that applies each estimator to its selected subset and combines the outputs. Transformer names are generated automatically from estimator types, while remainder controls what happens to unspecified columns.

parameters.name: transformers
parameters.description: Tuples of (transformer, columns); transformer may be an estimator, 'drop', or 'passthrough', and columns identify the data subset.

parameters.name: remainder
parameters.description: Controls processing of columns not listed in transformers: 'drop', 'passthrough', or an estimator; default is 'drop'.

parameters.name: sparse_threshold
parameters.description: Threshold used to decide whether the combined output is sparse; default is 0.3.

parameters.name: n_jobs
parameters.description: Number of jobs used for fitting and transforming; default is None.

parameters.name: verbose
parameters.description: Whether to print progress messages; default is False.

parameters.name: verbose_feature_names_out
parameters.description: Whether generated feature names include transformer names; default is True.

example.title: Build a mixed-column preprocessor
example.code:
from sklearn.compose import make_column_transformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

preprocessor = make_column_transformer(
    (StandardScaler(), ["age"]),
    (OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["city"]),
    remainder="drop",
)
example.explanation: Creates a transformer that scales the numeric column and one-hot encodes the categorical column; other columns are discarded.

interview.question: What does make_column_transformer simplify?
interview.answer: It is a convenience wrapper around the ColumnTransformer constructor. It creates transformer names automatically from the types of the supplied estimators, so callers provide transformer-and-column tuples without explicit names.
interview.followUp: What happens to columns omitted from those tuples? By default they are dropped; remainder='passthrough' retains them, or an estimator processes them.

interview.question: What can each transformer tuple contain?
interview.answer: Each tuple has the form (transformer, columns). The transformer can be an estimator, 'drop', or 'passthrough', and an estimator must support fit and transform.
interview.followUp: How can selections be generalized? Use selectors such as make_column_selector to choose columns by name pattern or data type.

interview.question: What object does the function return?
interview.answer: The function returns a ColumnTransformer object. That object applies the configured operations to the selected subsets and combines their results into one output.
interview.followUp: How is output sparsity controlled? The returned ColumnTransformer exposes sparse_threshold, which determines whether a combined sparse result is returned.

keyPoints: Use the function to assemble column-specific preprocessing into a ColumnTransformer.
Unlike the constructor, it does not accept explicit transformer names.
Generated names are derived from each transformer’s type.
Pass one tuple per operation, pairing a transformer with the columns it should receive.
Column selection can be delegated to make_column_selector when names or dtypes determine the subsets.
Set remainder to passthrough to preserve columns not covered by explicit transformer tuples.
Retained remainder columns are concatenated with transformed outputs.
gotchas: Unlisted columns are discarded unless remainder is set to passthrough or to an estimator.
A remainder estimator must implement both fit and transform.

make_pipeline.summary: Constructs a scikit-learn Pipeline from estimators supplied in order. It automatically generates lowercase step names from estimator types.
make_pipeline.explanation: Pass transformers and a final estimator in execution order. The function builds a Pipeline, automatically deriving each step name by lowercasing its estimator type; the resulting pipeline can be fitted and used for prediction as a single estimator.

parameters.name: steps
parameters.description: Ordered estimator objects to chain into the pipeline.

parameters.name: memory
parameters.description: Cache location or a joblib.Memory-compatible object; default=None.

parameters.name: verbose
parameters.description: Whether to print elapsed fitting time for each step; default=False.

example.title: Scale features and classify
example.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=200))
model.fit(X, y)
print(model.predict(X[:3]))
example.explanation: Standardizes the features and then fits a logistic-regression classifier as one estimator.

interview.question: What does make_pipeline provide compared with Pipeline?
interview.answer: make_pipeline accepts a variable number of estimators and returns a Pipeline containing them in the supplied order. It automatically names each step from the lowercase estimator type, so explicit step names are not provided.
interview.followUp: When are explicit names preferable? Use Pipeline when stable, custom names are needed for parameter searches or inspection.

interview.question: How are the supplied estimators used?
interview.answer: The steps are chained sequentially: transformers process the data before the final estimator receives it. The returned Pipeline exposes the composite estimator interface, including fitting and prediction when its last step supports those operations.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect a particular step? Access the pipeline's named_steps or steps attributes.

interview.question: What does the memory parameter do?
interview.answer: memory accepts a path or an object implementing the joblib.Memory interface. It caches fitted transformers, while caching is disabled by default and the final step is excluded from caching.
interview.followUp: What additional behavior should be considered when caching? Transformer instances are cloned before fitting, so inspect the fitted pipeline steps.

keyPoints: The function creates a Pipeline from the estimators passed as positional steps.
Step names are generated automatically by lowercasing each estimator's type name.
The positional steps form an ordered chain of scikit-learn estimators.
The memory option can cache fitted transformer steps.
verbose=True prints elapsed fitting time after each step completes.
gotchas: Enabling memory caching does not cache the final pipeline step.
With memory caching enabled, inspect the fitted clones through the pipeline rather than relying on the original transformer objects.

interview.question: What does make_regression generate?
interview.answer: make_regression generates synthetic regression data by applying a random linear model to generated features, using n_informative nonzero regressors. It can also add Gaussian noise to the outputs.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect the true model? Set coef=True and capture the third returned value, which contains the underlying coefficients.

interview.question: What shapes does the function return?
interview.answer: X has shape (n_samples, n_features). y has shape (n_samples,) for one target or (n_samples, n_targets) for multiple targets.
interview.followUp: What changes when n_targets is greater than one? The target matrix becomes two-dimensional, with one column per generated target.

interview.question: How do reproducibility and coefficient output work?
interview.answer: random_state controls the random generation and makes results reproducible when given a fixed integer. The function returns X and y by default, and additionally coefficients when coef=True.
interview.followUp: How can you create a noisy but reproducible problem? Pass both a nonzero noise value and a fixed random_state.

keyPoints: Use it to create controlled synthetic data for testing regression algorithms.
The default feature design is well conditioned; effective_rank and tail_strength can create a low-rank, fat-tailed structure.
Targets come from a random linear model, with bias allowing a nonzero intercept-like offset.
n_informative determines how many features receive nonzero coefficients in the generated model.
noise adds centered Gaussian variation to the target values, with its scale set by the noise argument.
shuffle independently controls whether generated samples and feature positions are randomized.
gotchas: The third return value is available only when coef=True; otherwise unpack just X and y.
noise controls the noise standard deviation, so nonzero noise makes generated targets differ from the noiseless linear relationship.
With shuffle=False, samples and features retain their generated ordering rather than being shuffled.

matthews_corrcoef.summary: Computes the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) for binary or multiclass classification. The score ranges from -1 for inverse prediction to +1 for perfect prediction, with 0 representing average random prediction.
matthews_corrcoef.explanation: The function compares ground-truth labels with classifier predictions and returns a correlation-style classification score. It supports binary and multiclass targets, incorporates sample weights when supplied, and ranges from -1 for inverse prediction through 0 for random performance to +1 for perfect prediction.

parameters.name: y_true
parameters.description: Ground truth (correct) target values.

parameters.name: y_pred
parameters.description: Estimated targets as returned by a classifier.

parameters.name: sample_weight
parameters.description: Sample weights.

example.title: Compute a binary MCC
example.code:
from sklearn.metrics import matthews_corrcoef

y_true = [1, 1, 1, -1]
y_pred = [1, -1, 1, 1]
score = matthews_corrcoef(y_true, y_pred)
print(score)  # -0.33
example.explanation: This computes the MCC for four binary predictions and prints the resulting score.

interview.question: What does matthews_corrcoef measure, and how do you interpret its range?
interview.answer: It returns the Matthews correlation coefficient, a balanced classification-quality measure that accounts for prediction errors and is useful when class sizes differ. Its range is -1 to +1: +1 is perfect prediction, 0 is average random prediction, and -1 is inverse prediction.
interview.followUp: What does the binary formula use? It combines true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives as �(tp�tn - fp�fn) divided by �sqrt((tp+fp)(tp+fn)(tn+fp)(tn+fn)).

interview.question: What are the function's parameters?
interview.answer: Pass y_true as the correct target values and y_pred as the estimated targets returned by a classifier. Both are array-like with shape (n_samples), and sample_weight can optionally assign a weight to each sample.
interview.followUp: Why might sample weights matter? They let evaluation give different importance to observations, which is useful when examples have unequal relevance or representation.

interview.question: Does the function support multiclass classification?
interview.answer: The function supports both binary and multiclass labels. In the binary case, the score is directly connected to the four confusion-matrix counts; the documentation does not restrict the function to binary targets.
interview.followUp: How should a multiclass score be interpreted? Treat it as the documented multiclass MCC rather than attempting to read it as a binary true-positive/negative statistic.

keyPoints: Use MCC to evaluate both binary and multiclass classifier predictions.
The metric incorporates the main prediction-error categories and remains balanced when class distributions are very uneven.
Interpret the result as a bounded correlation-like value from -1 to +1.
A score of +1 means perfect predictions, 0 indicates average random performance, and -1 indicates inverse predictions.
Both binary and multiclass target-label formats are accepted.
gotchas: Interpretations based directly on true and false positives and negatives apply only to binary classification; multiclass use is supported but has a different interpretation.

MaxAbsScaler.summary: MaxAbsScaler scales each feature by its largest absolute training value. It preserves zero-centered structure and sparsity because it does not subtract feature means.
MaxAbsScaler.explanation: MaxAbsScaler learns the largest absolute value in each feature during fit and uses those values to scale later data. It does not subtract feature means, so zero values remain zero; this also lets it preserve sparsity for supported sparse inputs.

parameters.name: copy
parameters.description: Whether to copy the input before transforming; default is True.

parameters.name: clip
parameters.description: Whether to clip transformed values to the fitted range; default is False.

MaxAbsScaler.returns: Transformed data with the same shape as the input; the class page documents transform as returning an array or sparse matrix.

example.title: Scale centered data
example.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import MaxAbsScaler

X = [[1., -1., 2.], [2., 0., 0.], [0., 1., -1.]]
scaler = MaxAbsScaler().fit(X)
X_scaled = scaler.transform(X)
print(X_scaled)
example.explanation: Fits per-feature maximum absolute values, then transforms the data by dividing each feature by its fitted maximum.

useCases.title: Zero-centered numeric data
useCases.scenario: Features are already centered around zero and need comparable magnitudes without mean subtraction.

useCases.title: Sparse feature matrices

interview.question: How does MaxAbsScaler transform features?
interview.answer: It divides each feature by that feature's maximum absolute training value, making the largest magnitude equal to 1. It does not center the features.
interview.followUp: Why can it preserve sparse structure? Because it scales existing values without subtracting a mean, so stored zero entries remain zero.

interview.question: How should it be used in a train/test workflow?
interview.answer: Call fit or fit_transform on training data, then call transform on new data. The learned per-feature scales are reused for later inputs.
interview.followUp: What leakage risk must be avoided? Fit only on the training partition; fitting before the split lets test information influence the learned scales.

interview.question: When is MaxAbsScaler a suitable choice?
interview.answer: It supports sparse CSR and CSC matrices and is intended for data already centered at zero or sparse data. Unlike a centering transformer, it does not destroy sparsity.
interview.followUp: When might another scaler be preferable? Use one with centering or robust statistics when zero-centered scaling is inappropriate or outliers need stronger treatment.

keyPoints: Each feature receives its own scale based on the largest absolute training value.
After fitting and transforming the training set, every feature's maximum magnitude is 1.
The transformation keeps the original zero locations because no mean is subtracted.
CSR and CSC sparse matrices are supported inputs.
fit learns the values needed by subsequent transform calls.
The estimator performs feature-wise, rather than global, normalization.
gotchas: It does not make outliers less influential; an extreme value still determines the feature's scale.
Do not use it when mean-centering is required; its design deliberately leaves feature offsets unchanged.
Sparse support is specific to CSR and CSC matrix formats documented on the class page.

Metric mode preserves quantitative distances, whereas nonmetric mode uses the rank order of dissimilarities; repeated initializations can improve the selected solution.

interview.question: What problem does `MDS` solve?
interview.answer: MDS is a manifold-learning estimator for embedding dissimilarities into a chosen number of dimensions. It supports metric and nonmetric modes and optimizes the embedding with SMACOF.
interview.followUp: How would you supply distances rather than feature vectors? Set `dissimilarity='precomputed'` and pass the square dissimilarity matrix to `fit` or `fit_transform`.

interview.question: Why might you increase `n_init`?
interview.answer: `n_init` controls how many SMACOF runs use different initializations. The estimator can run those initializations in parallel when appropriate, and the resulting solution is selected using stress.
interview.followUp: How can reproducibility be improved? Provide a fixed `random_state`, while remembering that changing initialization can change the optimization result.

interview.question: What do `n_components` and `dissimilarity` control?
interview.answer: `n_components` specifies the dimensionality of the embedding, while `dissimilarity` selects either pairwise Euclidean distances computed from the input or distances supplied directly. The default dissimilarity is Euclidean.
interview.followUp: When should precomputed distances be used? Use them when the pairwise relationship is not adequately represented by Euclidean distances in the original feature space.

keyPoints: Use `n_components` to choose how many coordinates each observation receives in the embedding.
Increase `n_init` to try multiple starting configurations and reduce dependence on one initialization.
`max_iter` bounds the optimization work performed by each individual SMACOF run.
`eps` determines when an optimization run is considered converged based on relative stress improvement.
Set `metric_mds` to select quantitative-distance preservation or rank-based nonmetric embedding.
`n_jobs` can control parallel execution of multiple initialization runs.
gotchas: In nonmetric mode, zero dissimilarities are treated as missing values, so zero entries should not be used to represent genuine equal distances.
Interpret the `stress_` value according to the selected mode: metric MDS defaults to raw stress, while nonmetric MDS defaults to normalized stress.

mean_absolute_error.summary: Computes mean absolute error, a non-negative regression loss based on absolute differences between true and predicted targets. It can weight samples and either preserve or aggregate errors across multiple outputs.
mean_absolute_error.explanation: The function compares each predicted target with its corresponding true target, takes the absolute error, and averages it. For multiple outputs, it can return one error per output or aggregate outputs uniformly or with supplied weights; sample weights can also affect the averaging.

parameters.name: y_true
parameters.description: Ground-truth target values; array-like with shape `(n_samples,)` or `(n_samples, n_outputs)`.

parameters.name: y_pred
parameters.description: Estimated target values; array-like with shape `(n_samples,)` or `(n_samples, n_outputs)`.

parameters.name: sample_weight
parameters.description: Sample weights; array-like with shape `(n_samples,)`, default `None`.

parameters.name: multioutput
parameters.description: Output aggregation mode: `'raw_values'`, `'uniform_average'`, or an array-like of output weights; default `'uniform_average'`.

mean_absolute_error.returns: float or array of floats. `raw_values` returns one error per output; uniform aggregation or an output-weight array returns a weighted average. The result is non-negative, with 0.0 as the best value.

example.title: Compute a regression error
example.code:
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error

y_true = [3, -0.5, 2, 7]
y_pred = [2.5, 0.0, 2, 8]

mae = mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)
print(mae)  # 0.5
example.explanation: This computes the scalar MAE for four regression predictions.

interview.question: What does mean_absolute_error measure?
interview.answer: It is a regression loss that returns a non-negative floating-point value. A perfect prediction has a score of 0.0.
interview.followUp: How can multiple outputs be handled? Use `raw_values` for separate output errors, or use uniform aggregation or an output-weight array for one combined result.

interview.question: What are the main input arguments?
interview.answer: `y_true` contains the correct target values and `y_pred` contains estimated target values. Both may be one-dimensional or shaped for multiple outputs.
interview.followUp: How would sample-level importance be represented? Pass an array of sample weights through `sample_weight`.

interview.question: How does the multioutput argument change the return value?
interview.answer: With `multioutput='raw_values'`, the function returns an error for each output. With the default uniform aggregation or an output-weight array, it returns one weighted average.
interview.followUp: What does `sample_weight` control? It supplies weights used when averaging the sample errors.

keyPoints: This function is a regression loss based on absolute prediction errors.
Scores cannot be negative, and lower values indicate better predictions; zero is optimal.
Pass the reference targets as `y_true`.
Pass the model's predictions as `y_pred`.
The `multioutput` argument controls how errors from several target columns are combined.
gotchas: Use `raw_values` when you need an error for every output instead of one aggregate score.
An array supplied to `multioutput` must represent output-combination weights, not per-sample weights.

mean_squared_error.summary: Computes mean squared error, a regression loss that summarizes squared differences between true and predicted targets. It returns one aggregate value by default or per-output values when requested.
mean_squared_error.explanation: The function compares each predicted target with its corresponding true target, squares the differences, and averages them. For multiple outputs, it can either return one error per output or combine output errors using uniform or user-supplied weights; sample weights can also influence the calculation.

parameters.name: y_pred

parameters.name: sample_weight
parameters.description: Optional sample weights; array-like with shape (n_samples,).

parameters.name: multioutput
parameters.description: Output aggregation mode: 'raw_values', 'uniform_average', or an array-like of shape (n_outputs,) containing output weights.

mean_squared_error.returns: A non-negative float, or an array of floats with one value for each individual target.

example.title: Compute mean squared error
example.code:
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

y_true = [3, -0.5, 2, 7]
y_pred = [2.5, 0.0, 2, 8]

print(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))  # 0.375

interview.question: What does mean_squared_error measure?
interview.answer: It computes a regression loss by averaging squared differences between corresponding true and predicted values. Lower values are better, and the best value is 0.0.
interview.followUp: How can multiple outputs be handled? Use multioutput='raw_values' for one error per target, or aggregate them with uniform or custom output weights.

interview.question: What shapes do the target arguments support?
interview.answer: y_true and y_pred contain the ground-truth and estimated target values. Each can have shape (n_samples,) for one output or (n_samples, n_outputs) for multiple outputs.
interview.followUp: What additional weighting is available? sample_weight assigns weights to individual samples, while multioutput controls aggregation across targets.

interview.question: How does multioutput affect the return value?
interview.answer: The default multioutput='uniform_average' averages output errors equally. 'raw_values' returns an array containing the error for each output, and an array-like value supplies custom output weights.
interview.followUp: When would raw_values be preferable? It is useful when each target's error must be inspected independently rather than reduced to one scalar.

keyPoints: This function is a regression loss based on squared prediction errors.
y_true supplies the correct target values used for comparison.
y_pred supplies the model's estimated target values.
multioutput determines how errors from several target columns are combined.
The default aggregation gives every output equal influence.
gotchas: The metric cannot be negative; a value of zero indicates the best possible result.
When providing multiple output weights, the array must define how output errors are combined.

MeanShift.summary: MeanShift performs unsupervised clustering with a flat kernel, automatically discovering cluster centers from sample density. It updates candidate centroids toward local means and removes near-duplicate candidates.
MeanShift.explanation: MeanShift starts kernel candidates from seeds or a binning scheme, repeatedly moves each candidate toward the mean of nearby samples, then removes nearly duplicate candidates. The surviving centroids define the clusters, while labels associate samples with them; the number of clusters is determined by the data rather than supplied directly.
MeanShift.syntax: class sklearn.cluster.MeanShift(*, bandwidth=None, seeds=None, bin_seeding=False, min_bin_freq=1, cluster_all=True, n_jobs=None, max_iter=300)

parameters.name: bandwidth
parameters.description: Flat-kernel bandwidth; when omitted, it is estimated with estimate_bandwidth.

parameters.name: seeds
parameters.description: Kernel initialization points.

parameters.name: bin_seeding
parameters.description: Whether to use discretized, binned points as initial kernel locations.

parameters.name: min_bin_freq
parameters.description: Minimum number of points required in a bin when generating seed locations.

parameters.name: cluster_all
parameters.description: Whether every sample must receive a cluster assignment, including orphan points.

parameters.name: max_iter
parameters.description: Maximum number of iterations per seed.

parameters.name: n_jobs
parameters.description: Number of parallel jobs; None means the default job behavior.

MeanShift.returns: Fitted estimator with cluster_centers_ containing the coordinates of cluster centers and labels_ containing the label of each sample.

example.title: Cluster points with an explicit bandwidth
example.code:
from sklearn.cluster import MeanShift

X = [[1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1], [8, 8], [8, 9], [9, 8]]
model = MeanShift(bandwidth=2).fit(X)

print(model.labels_)
print(model.cluster_centers_)
example.explanation: Fits MeanShift to two separated groups and prints the assigned labels and learned centroids.

useCases.title: Density-based exploratory clustering
useCases.scenario: You have unlabeled vector data whose groups correspond to dense regions and do not want to choose the number of clusters first.

useCases.title: Mode or centroid discovery

useCases.title: Binned initialization for scalability
